topics.title: The long history of Indian farming

learn.hook: Farmers in the Indian subcontinent have been growing crops for thousands of years. Some of their ideas are still used today!
points: Mehrgarh, at the foot of the Bolan Pass (in present-day Pakistan), is one of the earliest known farming villages in the subcontinent. People there grew wheat and barley and kept cattle, sheep and goats.
Harappan farmers grew wheat, barley, pulses and cotton. Remains of a ploughed field have been found at Kalibangan in Rajasthan.
Ancient texts such as the Kṛiṣhi-Parāshara give advice on rain, seeds, ploughing and caring for cattle. The Vṛikṣhāyurveda deals with the care of plants and trees.
The Kallaṇai (Grand Anicut) across the Kaveri, built by the Chola king Karikāla about 2,000 years ago, is one of the oldest water-diversion structures in the world still in use.

In the 1960s, the Green Revolution brought high-yielding varieties of wheat and rice, with more irrigation and fertilisers, greatly increasing harvests, especially in Punjab and Haryana. Dr M. S. Swaminathan was a leading scientist of this effort.

example.q: The Kallaṇai on the Kaveri has been used for about 2,000 years. What does this tell us about early Tamil farmers?
steps: The dam diverts river water into channels for fields.
Building something that lasts 2,000 years needs great engineering skill.
So early farmers and rulers understood rivers and water management very well.
example.answer: That they had advanced knowledge of water management and engineering for farming.

learn.reallife: In many villages, farmers still read the sky, winds and birds to predict rain, carrying forward knowledge from very old times.

quiz.q: Which is one of the earliest known farming villages in the Indian subcontinent?
quiz.explain: Mehrgarh, near the Bolan Pass, shows very early farming of wheat and barley.
steps: Mehrgarh lies at the foot of the Bolan Pass, in present-day Pakistan.
It is one of the earliest known farming villages in the subcontinent.
Pāṭaliputra, Delhi and Kochi are much later cities.
Answer: Mehrgarh
quiz.mistake: Picks a later city

quiz.q: Which crops were grown at Mehrgarh?
quiz.explain: Early farmers at Mehrgarh grew wheat and barley.
steps: Early farmers at Mehrgarh grew cereals and kept cattle, sheep and goats.
The cereals were wheat and barley.
Potatoes, tomatoes, tea and coffee came to India much later.
Answer: Wheat and barley
quiz.mistake: Picks crops brought to India much later

quiz.q: Remains of a ploughed field from Harappan times were found at:
quiz.explain: Kalibangan in Rajasthan shows a ploughed field with furrows.
steps: Harappan farmers ploughed their fields.
Remains of a ploughed field were found at Kalibangan in Rajasthan.
Ajanta, Sarnath and Thanjavur are not Harappan sites.
Answer: Kalibangan
quiz.mistake: Mixes up Harappan sites with later ones

quiz.q: Who built the Kallaṇai (Grand Anicut) across the Kaveri?
quiz.explain: The Chola king Karikāla built it about 2,000 years ago.
steps: The Kallaṇai (Grand Anicut) is across the Kaveri.
It was built by the Chola king Karikāla about 2,000 years ago.
Ashoka, Samudragupta and Kanishka were northern rulers.
Answer: Karikāla Chola
quiz.mistake: Credits a northern ruler with a southern work

quiz.q: The Kṛiṣhi-Parāshara is an ancient text about:
quiz.explain: It gives advice on rain, seeds, ploughing and cattle care.
steps: 'Kṛiṣhi' means farming.
The Kṛiṣhi-Parāshara gives advice on rain, seeds, ploughing and cattle care.
So it is about agriculture.
Answer: Agriculture
quiz.mistake: Guesses the subject without knowing 'kṛiṣhi' means farming

quiz.q: The Green Revolution of the 1960s mainly increased the production of:
quiz.explain: High-yielding wheat and rice varieties greatly increased grain harvests.
steps: The Green Revolution brought high-yielding varieties of grain.
These were wheat and rice.
So it mainly increased wheat and rice production.
Answer: Wheat and rice
quiz.mistake: Thinks it was about other products

quiz.q: Which states gained most in the early years of the Green Revolution?
quiz.explain: Punjab and Haryana had good irrigation and adopted the new seeds quickly.
steps: The Green Revolution needed good irrigation and new seeds.
Punjab and Haryana had these and gained most in the early years.
So the answer is Punjab and Haryana.
Answer: Punjab and Haryana
quiz.mistake: Does not know where the Green Revolution began

quiz.q: Which scientist is closely linked with India's Green Revolution?
quiz.explain: Dr M. S. Swaminathan led work on high-yielding varieties in India.
steps: A leading scientist worked on high-yielding varieties in India.
That scientist was Dr M. S. Swaminathan.
C. V. Raman and Homi Bhabha worked in physics.
Answer: Dr M. S. Swaminathan
quiz.mistake: Picks a famous scientist from another field

teach.ask: Gappu thinks farming in India began recently. Tell him the long story of Indian farming.
teach.praise: From Mehrgarh to the Green Revolution! Indian farmers have been clever for thousands of years.
teach.nudge: Good! Can you tell me about a very old farming place, or about the Green Revolution?

revise.summary: Farming in India is very old: Mehrgarh grew wheat and barley, Harappans ploughed fields at Kalibangan, texts like the Kṛiṣhi-Parāshara guided farmers, and Karikāla Chola built the Kallaṇai. The 1960s Green Revolution boosted wheat and rice.
focus: Know early farming sites: Mehrgarh and Kalibangan
Know the Kallaṇai and who built it
Explain the Green Revolution and Dr M. S. Swaminathan
remember: Mehrgarh (near the Bolan Pass): wheat, barley, cattle, sheep, goats
Kṛiṣhi-Parāshara: farming advice; Vṛikṣhāyurveda: care of plants
Kallaṇai on the Kaveri, by Karikāla Chola, about 2,000 years ago; Green Revolution 1960s, Punjab and Haryana
traps: The Kallaṇai was built by a Chola king, not a northern ruler
Don't link the Green Revolution with tea or coffee; it was about wheat and rice
Tea, coffee and potatoes were not early Mehrgarh crops

learn.hook: Rice loves the rainy season, while wheat likes cool winters. Indian farmers plan their year around crop seasons.
points: India has three main crop seasons. Kharif crops are sown with the monsoon (June–July) and harvested in September–October: rice, maize, cotton, jowar, bajra, groundnut and soybean.
Rabi crops are sown in winter (October–December) and harvested in spring (March–April): wheat, barley, gram (chana), mustard and peas.
Zaid crops are grown in the short summer season between rabi and kharif: watermelon, muskmelon, cucumber and some vegetables and fodder.
Soils differ: alluvial soil in the Northern Plains is very fertile; black soil (regur) of the Deccan holds moisture and is ideal for cotton; red soil gets its colour from iron.
Laterite soil forms in areas of high temperature and heavy rain and suits crops like cashew, tea and coffee; desert soil in Rajasthan is sandy and suits hardy crops like bajra.

example.q: A farmer in Punjab grows rice from June to October and wheat from November to April. Which crop seasons is she using?
steps: Rice is sown with the monsoon and harvested in autumn: that is kharif.
Wheat is sown in winter and harvested in spring: that is rabi.
Using both seasons lets her grow two crops a year on the same land.
example.answer: Rice is a kharif crop and wheat is a rabi crop.

learn.reallife: Watermelons piled high on carts in May are zaid crops, grown in the short summer season.

quiz.q: Kharif crops are sown:
options: With the arrival of the monsoon
quiz.explain: Kharif crops are sown in June–July when monsoon rains begin.
steps: Kharif crops are sown in June–July.
That is when the monsoon arrives.
Rabi crops are sown in winter.
Answer: With the arrival of the monsoon
quiz.mistake: Mixes up kharif and rabi seasons

quiz.q: Which is a rabi crop?
quiz.explain: Wheat is sown in winter and harvested in spring, so it is rabi.
steps: Rabi crops are sown in winter and harvested in spring.
Wheat is grown this way.
Rice, cotton and maize are kharif crops.
Answer: Wheat
quiz.mistake: Thinks wheat grows in the rainy season

quiz.q: Which is a kharif crop?
quiz.explain: Rice needs a lot of water and is grown in the monsoon season.
steps: Kharif crops grow in the monsoon season.
Rice needs a lot of water and is a kharif crop.
Wheat, mustard and gram are rabi crops.
Answer: Rice
quiz.mistake: Mixes up rice with winter crops

quiz.q: Watermelon and cucumber grown in the short summer season are:
quiz.explain: Zaid crops grow between the rabi and kharif seasons.
steps: Watermelon and cucumber grow in the short summer season.
That season lies between rabi and kharif.
Its crops are called zaid crops.
Answer: Zaid crops
quiz.mistake: Does not know the third crop season

quiz.q: Black soil is especially good for growing:
quiz.explain: Black soil holds moisture well and is ideal for cotton; it is also called black cotton soil.
steps: Black soil (regur) of the Deccan holds moisture well.
It is ideal for cotton, so it is called black cotton soil.
So the answer is cotton.
Answer: Cotton
quiz.mistake: Does not link black soil with cotton

quiz.q: Why is red soil red?
options: It has a lot of coal
quiz.explain: Iron compounds give red soil its colour.
steps: Soils get colours from what they contain.
Red soil gets its colour from iron.
So red soil is red because it contains iron.
Answer: It contains iron
quiz.mistake: Does not know what colours the soil

quiz.q: The most fertile soil of the Northern Plains is:
quiz.explain: Rivers deposited fine alluvium across the Northern Plains.
steps: Rivers deposited fine soil across the Northern Plains.
This alluvial soil is very fertile.
Desert and laterite soils are found elsewhere.
Answer: Alluvial soil
quiz.mistake: Mixes up soil types and regions

quiz.q: Rabi crops are usually harvested in:
quiz.explain: Rabi crops sown in winter are harvested in spring, around March–April.
steps: Rabi crops are sown in winter (October–December).
They are harvested in spring.
That is around March–April.
Answer: March–April
quiz.mistake: Confuses the rabi harvest with the kharif harvest

teach.ask: Gappu wants to plant seeds but doesn't know when. Explain the crop seasons and soils of India.
teach.praise: Kharif with the rains, rabi in winter and zaid in summer, and the right soil for each crop. I'm ready to plant!
teach.nudge: Good! Which season is wheat grown in, and which is rice grown in?

revise.summary: India has three crop seasons: kharif (sown with the monsoon, like rice and cotton), rabi (sown in winter, like wheat and gram) and zaid (short summer, like watermelon). Soils differ: alluvial, black, red, laterite and desert.
focus: Tell kharif, rabi and zaid crops apart
Know when each season's crops are sown and harvested
Match soils with their regions and crops
Explain what gives soils their features
remember: Kharif: sown June–July, harvested Sept–Oct (rice, maize, cotton, jowar, bajra)
Rabi: sown Oct–Dec, harvested March–April (wheat, barley, gram, mustard, peas)
Alluvial: Northern Plains; black (regur): cotton; red: iron; laterite: cashew, tea, coffee
traps: Don't swap the seasons: wheat is rabi, rice is kharif
Rabi crops are harvested in spring, not autumn
Black soil suits cotton, not tea

topics.title: Water, farming practices and farmers' challenges

learn.hook: A drip of water at the root of each plant can save far more water than flooding a whole field. Smart farming saves water!
points: Irrigation means supplying water to crops. Sources include canals, wells and tube-wells, tanks and ponds. Traditional systems include stepwells, johads in Rajasthan, kuhls in Himachal Pradesh and bamboo drip irrigation in Meghalaya.
Drip and sprinkler irrigation give water only where it is needed, saving a great deal of water.
Good practices: crop rotation (growing pulses after cereals helps restore soil fertility), mixed cropping, using compost and manure, and terrace farming on hill slopes to stop soil from washing away.
Many farmers face challenges: small landholdings, dependence on the monsoon, falling groundwater levels, soil damage from overuse of chemicals, and uncertain prices for crops.
The government supports farmers through Minimum Support Prices (MSP) for some crops, Soil Health Cards, crop insurance and farm loans through Kisan Credit Cards.

example.q: A farmer grows rice and wheat on the same field year after year and the soil is getting weaker. What change could help?
steps: Growing the same cereal crops again and again uses up the same nutrients.
Pulses such as moong or chana help restore nitrogen in the soil.
So rotating crops, by growing pulses in between, can make the soil healthier.
example.answer: Practise crop rotation, for example by growing pulses between cereal crops.

learn.reallife: The step-like terraced fields you may see in pictures of Uttarakhand, Sikkim or Meghalaya are an example of farming adapted to hill slopes.

games.title: Farming: true or false?
items: Drip irrigation saves water compared with flooding fields.
Water goes only to the plant roots.
Growing pulses can help improve soil fertility.
Pulses help add nitrogen to the soil.
Terrace farming helps stop soil from washing down slopes.
All Indian farmers have very large farms.
Using too many chemical fertilisers can harm the soil.
Overuse can damage soil health over time.
MSP means the government buys all crops at any price farmers ask.
MSP is a fixed minimum price announced for certain crops.

quiz.q: Which irrigation method saves the most water?
options: Watering at noon on bare soil
quiz.explain: Drip irrigation delivers water directly to the roots, wasting very little.
steps: Drip irrigation gives water only where it is needed, at the roots.
Flooding and open taps waste water.
So drip irrigation saves the most water.
Answer: Drip irrigation
quiz.mistake: Thinks more water always means better farming

quiz.q: Why do farmers in hilly areas make terraces?
options: To create flat steps and stop soil from washing away
quiz.explain: Terraces slow rainwater and hold soil on slopes.
steps: On hill slopes, rain can wash soil away.
Terraces make flat steps that slow the water and hold the soil.
So terraces stop soil from washing away.
Answer: To create flat steps and stop soil from washing away
quiz.mistake: Does not see the link between slopes and soil erosion

quiz.q: Crop rotation means:
options: Growing different crops on a field in different seasons
Moving the farm to a new place
quiz.explain: Changing crops helps the soil recover nutrients.
steps: Crop rotation means changing crops on a field.
Different crops are grown in different seasons, like pulses after cereals.
This helps the soil recover.
Answer: Growing different crops on a field in different seasons
quiz.mistake: Takes 'rotation' literally

quiz.q: Which crops help restore nitrogen to the soil?
quiz.explain: Pulse plants help add nitrogen to the soil.
steps: Growing pulses after cereals helps restore soil fertility.
Pulse plants like moong and chana add nitrogen to the soil.
So the answer is pulses like moong and chana.
Answer: Pulses like moong and chana
quiz.mistake: Thinks all crops affect soil in the same way

quiz.q: Johads are traditional water-harvesting structures of:
quiz.explain: Johads collect and store rainwater in dry Rajasthan.
steps: Traditional water systems: johads (Rajasthan), kuhls (Himachal Pradesh), bamboo drip (Meghalaya).
Johads collect and store rainwater in dry Rajasthan.
So the answer is Rajasthan.
Answer: Rajasthan
quiz.mistake: Mixes up traditional systems of different regions

quiz.q: Which is a challenge faced by many Indian farmers?
options: Too much land and too little work
Small landholdings and dependence on the monsoon
quiz.explain: Most farmers have small plots and many depend on monsoon rains.
steps: Farmers face small landholdings, dependence on the monsoon, falling groundwater and uncertain prices.
'Small landholdings and dependence on the monsoon' are real challenges.
The other options are not true problems.
Answer: Small landholdings and dependence on the monsoon
quiz.mistake: Does not know the real difficulties of farming

quiz.q: What does a Soil Health Card tell a farmer?
options: The nutrients in their soil and what to add
The number of cows in the village
quiz.explain: It shows the soil's nutrient status and suggests fertilisers or manure.
steps: A Soil Health Card is given to farmers by the government.
It shows the nutrients in their soil.
It suggests what fertiliser or manure to add.
Answer: The nutrients in their soil and what to add
quiz.mistake: Does not know what the card is for

quiz.q: MSP stands for:
quiz.explain: MSP is the minimum price at which the government offers to buy certain crops.
steps: MSP is a support the government gives farmers.
It stands for Minimum Support Price.
It is the minimum price at which the government offers to buy certain crops.
Answer: Minimum Support Price
quiz.mistake: Guesses the expansion

teach.ask: Gappu wants to be a farmer. Tell him how to water crops wisely, care for the soil, and what problems farmers face.
teach.praise: Save water with drips, rotate crops, and know that the government helps too. Farming needs brains!

revise.summary: Irrigation brings water to crops through canals, wells, tanks and traditional systems like johads and kuhls; drip irrigation saves water. Good practices include crop rotation and terracing, and the government helps farmers through MSP, Soil Health Cards, insurance and loans.
focus: Name irrigation sources and traditional water systems
remember: Traditional systems: stepwells, johads (Rajasthan), kuhls (Himachal), bamboo drip (Meghalaya)
Drip and sprinkler irrigation save water
Crop rotation with pulses restores nitrogen; terraces stop soil erosion
MSP = Minimum Support Price; also Soil Health Cards, crop insurance, Kisan Credit Cards
traps: More water does not always mean better farming
Johads are from Rajasthan, not Kerala
MSP is a minimum price, not a maximum
